input: Given question: What does it mean by isovolumetric contraction of the heart? Option A: This is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers but there is a decrease in volume. Option B: This is when the atrium contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are open and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is no shortening of muscle fibers and the volume does not decrease. Option C: This is when the atrium contracts for the first 0.02-0.05s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers and there is no emptying. Option D: This is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.05s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the semilunar valves are open and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is no shortening of muscle fibers but emptying happens. Option E: This is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the semilunar valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers and there is no emptying. The correct answer is Option E.
reference: Isovolumetric/isometric basically means when the ventricles contract, increased pressure needs to build up before its gets higher than aortic/pulmonary pressure for the semilunar valves to open. During this period (of approximately 0.02-0.03s), there is no emptying and only little shortening of muscle fibers. The main point is that the volume in the ventricles DOES NOT change even though the intraventricular pressure rapidly increases. Reference Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 13th edition. Chapter 9 Cardiac Muscle, especially page 115 under subtitle Outflow of Blood From the Ventricles during Systole.

The initial closure of the valves marks the beginning of ventricular systole. From the onset of isovolumetric contraction until the closure of the valves, the ventricles are under pressure and volume does not change. This period is short, approximately 0.02-0.03 seconds, and its duration is dictated by the time required to build up pressure in the ventricles. During isovolumetransport contraction, the atria are contracting and the semilunar valves are closed, so there is no blood flow during this period. The pressure in the ventricles is building up and this is what will eventually result in valve closure. The ventricles do not empty during isovolumetransport contraction, but they do not fill either. The ventricular volume remains constant. Isovolumetransport contraction is sometimes referred to as "ventricular isovolumic contraction" or "ventricular systole before closure of the valves". The term "isovolumic" refers to the fact that volume is not changing during this phase of contraction. The contraction of the ventricles results in a decrease in volume, but this happens after valve closure during ventricular diastole. input: Given question: Your GI consultant presents to you a patient that has developed some Gastric ulcers. She tells you that they have ruled out the chances of a H.Pylori cause. The patient is of relatively normal weight and about 30, with no smoking history or alcohol misuse. Before you take a history, the consultant tells you that it is likely another extremely common cause of gastric ulcers, being... Option A: A Gastro-carcinoma Option B: Gastric Neoplasia Option C: Stress Option D: Crohn's Disease Option E: NSAIDS The correct answer is Option E.
reference: The inhibition of COX-1 enzymes via the action of non-specific NSAIDS. such as Ibuprofen and Aspirin,  results in a decrease in mucus lining is no longer being produced and the gastric lining is now vulnerable to gastric acid; this can result in gastric ulcers. Though you have not taken a history of the patient, NSAIDs are the second most common cause in the UK for gastric ulcers, after Helicobacter Pylori. Dr Green's lecture has the rough figures, with gastric carcinoma being 3rd most common and the other causes listed much rarer.
best_explanation:
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can cause gastric ulcers.  They inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, which protects the stomach.  Prostaglandins bind to EP3 receptors, which are G-protein coupled receptors.  The G-protein alpha subunit (Gαq/11) interacts with the phospholipase C (PLC) enzyme which catalyses the conversion of PIP2 -> DAG + IP3.  DAG activates Protein Kinase C, which phosphorylates and activates the enzyme COX. COX is responsible for prostaglandin synthesis.  So essentially, NSAIDs inhibit this process, leading to the formation of gastric ulcers.  For further information, see this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSkocizPFAA (from 25:38)  and this webpage: https://www.cancertherapyadvisor.com/home/decision-support-in-medicine/medicine-news-review/how-do-nsaids-cause-gastric-ulcers/article/689160/   (The first 500 words or so of the webpage is a good read for this question)  Hope this helps! Mesenchymal cells continue to migrate as blood vessels continue to proliferate.5. Consolidation: Callus calcifies + ends unite w/ bony callus. Chondrocytes undergo terminal differentiation + become apoptotic.6. Remodelling: woven bone is replaced w/ lamellar bone + excess bone resorbed. Takes years + is often incomplete. The doctor asks you which part is this? Option A: Anterior Fibromuscular stroma Option B: Central Option C: Oblique Option D: Peripheral Option E: Transitional The correct answer is Option E.
reference: The transitional zone is the correct answer. This zone surrounds the prostatic urethra, therefore would cause the symptoms of frequency. Diabetes could also cause frequent urination but there would also be high volumes of urine too.This is a question from page 8 of the Case 2 Anatomy booklet.

Subscapularis is innervated by the subscapular nerve.
